blocks.text: And the misty mouth of the Bosphorus and the ridges of Mysia appeared. Prose writers also use it: for example Polemo in Athenaeus, book 13, and another in the Suda; and Pausanias in the Laconica, where he speaks of Colona, a place in Sparta. In Hesychius κολώνη [kolōnē] is τόπος ὑψηλὸς, καὶ ἐπανάστημα γῆς βουνοειδὲς [topos hypsēlos, kai epanastēma gēs bounoeides], a lofty place, and an elevation of the ground in the manner of a mound. And in the scholiasts on Homer, τόπος εἰς ὕψος ἀνήκων, καὶ γεώλεφος ἐξοχὴ [topos eis hypsos anēkōn, kai geōlephos exochē], a place rising to a height, and a hilly prominence. The other conjecture is that גלים gallim is rendered here as χελώνας [chelōnas], or tortoises, following the usage of the Syriac language, in which ܓܠܐ gala is tortoise. Accordingly the Syriac here has ܐܝܟ ܓܠܐ, that is, like tortoises, according to Gabriel Sionita. And in the Syriac Lexicon of Giovanni Battista Ferrari, page 107, ܓܠܐ gala is rendered tortoise. Yet in the Thesaurus of Thomas of Novara, page 241, the Syriac words ܫܠܘܦܝܬܐ seluphita and ܥܓܠܐ gala are distinguished in such a way that the former signifies the tortoise in general, the latter only the male tortoise. This I think is more correct, since the Arabs call the same animal غيلم [ghaylam] gailam, surely in allusion to this word. So testify Giauhari, Alcamus, Damir and others. And the name is formed from lust. For غلم [ghalam] galam means lust, and the verb غلم [ghalima] galima means to burn with lust. That the male tortoise is rightly called غيلم [ghaylam] [col. 1092] gailam may be shown by these words of Aelian, Historia, book 15, chapter 19: Χερσαία χελώνη ζῶον λαγνίστατον· ἀλλὰ ὅγε ἄῤῥην. ὁμιλεῖ δὲ ἡ θήλεια ἄκουσα [Chersaia chelōnē zōon lagnistaton; alla hoge arrhēn. homilei de hē thēleia akousa]. The land tortoise is a most lustful animal; that is, its male: for the female mates only unwillingly. And Damostratus writes that she shrinks from mating for this reason: because, when she has been turned on her back by the male, she cannot right herself on account of the excessive weight of her shell, [II, 522] and after mating lies open as prey to the eagle and to other animals. But I think what others write is more correct, that in the very act of mating she suffers severe pain, because the male's member is hard and spiny. I pass over the fable of Damostratus, not omitted by Damir, about a certain unknown herb which the male holds in his mouth and so draws the resisting female to himself. Meanwhile, although not only for the Greeks but also for the Syriac and the Arabic translators גלים gallim in Hosea are tortoises, I nevertheless see no reason why we should depart from the received rendering of that passage. Everyone sees that the altars of the idols, met everywhere in the fields, are rightly compared with those heaps of stones we have mentioned, both on account of their cheapness and on account of their frequency. Not to mention that to those viewing them from afar their appearance is not dissimilar. But whatever is adduced to establish a likeness between these altars and tortoises is forced and far-fetched. Hosea's words can also be taken as spoken prophetically, as if he foretold that the altars of the people of Gilgal would shortly be כגלים, like heaps of stones that are in the fields, that is, would shortly be demolished. Nor should the allusion of the word Galgal to גלים gallim be neglected, so that Galgal and its altars are said to be destined to become like gallim, or heaps of stones. Just as in Sophon. II, 4: Aza (or Gaza) shall be עזובה (azuba) forsaken. And Accaron תעקר (theaker) shall be uprooted. As in the Pseudo-Sibyllines,
Καὶ Ῥώμη ῥύμη ἔσεται, καὶ Δῆλος ἄδηλος· [Kai Rhōmē rhymē esetai, kai Dēlos adēlos;]
and in the history of Susanna σχίσαι [schisai] and πρίσαι [prisai] allude to the names of the trees σχίνον [schinon] and πρίνον [prinon].
